item_name: HCS301 KeeLoq architecture and security boundaries
question_answered: What does public Microchip documentation establish about HCS301 code-word structure, synchronization, serial/discrimination data, crypt-key and seed roles, manufacturer-code domains, and the limits of passive observations, without providing attack procedures?
applicability_to_t5502_hcs301: Direct only if the requester's 8-pin device is confirmed as a genuine Microchip HCS301 or a functionally equivalent implementation using the same configured format. The architecture explains why a T5502 with such an encoder cannot be treated as a fixed-code remote. Hiland's public T5502 material does not name HCS301, so T5502-specific key derivation, seed use, baud selection, and receiver policy remain unverified.
authorization_assumption: Analysis is limited to an owned transmitter and authorized access-control system. Passive observations, enrollment, and service must not target third-party credentials or bypass an administrator's access policy.
key_findings: Primary-document fact: HCS301 transmits a 66-bit data word: a 32-bit encrypted/hopping portion plus a 34-bit fixed portion consisting of a 28-bit serial number, four button bits, and two status bits.

Primary-document fact: before encryption, the 32-bit hopping plaintext contains a 16-bit synchronization counter, ten discrimination bits, two overflow bits, and four button bits. The counter increments for each transmission.

Primary-document fact: the 64-bit per-transmitter crypt key is normally calculated/programmed during production; typical key generation uses the transmitter serial number and a secret 64-bit manufacturer code, but system designers can choose another matching derivation.
Primary-document fact: the 28-bit transmitted serial number is clear and intended to be unique; it identifies a learned transmitter but is not itself sufficient to authenticate the encrypted portion.

Primary-document fact: discrimination bits are checked after decryption to validate correct key use; typically they equal the ten least-significant serial bits, but a system may program and store another value.

Primary-document fact: HCS301 stores a two-word/32-bit seed and can transmit it under a special all-input combination for secure learning. The seed is an input to a receiver's key-generation process; it is not the 64-bit crypt key or manufacturer code.

Documentation conflict: DS21143C's glossary calls secure-learning seed data '60-bit,' but the same revision's EEPROM map, seed section, and code-word diagram consistently specify a 32-bit seed replacing the 32-bit encrypted portion. The 60-bit phrase is treated as a likely documentation error, not evidence of a second HCS301 seed width.

Security boundary: ordinary RF observations reveal fixed fields and changing ciphertext but do not disclose the protected key or the receiver's manufacturer-code/key-generation domain. A visible or transmitted seed, where an OEM deliberately enables that learn mode, still does not by itself establish the derivation method/domain or enroll a new serial.

System fact: a compatible receiver must learn a transmitter, derive or possess the appropriate key, decrypt/authenticate it, and store at least serial and synchronization state; normal acceptance also depends on a forward synchronization policy.

Feasibility conclusion: passive capture can identify and characterize a protocol, but cannot legitimately produce an independent accepted credential without OEM provisioning and/or receiver-authorized enrollment. Reusing observed traffic is specifically what the rolling counter and blocked window are designed to reject.
primary_sources: Microchip Technology, 'HCS301 KEELOQ Code Hopping Encoder,' DS21143C, Revision C, June 2011, https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/21143C.pdf (accessed 2026-10-01).

Microchip Technology, 'Remote Keyless Entry and Convenience Center Reference Design with LIN Bus Interface,' AN728, dated 2015-06-24 on current page, https://www.microchip.com/en-us/application-notes/an728 (accessed 2026-10-01).
secondary_sources: No secondary source is required for the architecture claims because Microchip's datasheet is authoritative. Third-party mirrors were consulted only to locate text and are not relied upon where the official PDF is available. Public academic cryptanalysis exists, but procedural attack material is outside this item's safe scope and intentionally omitted.
evidence_quality: High for bit widths, EEPROM roles, learning concepts, electrical limits, code-word construction, and typical decoder synchronization because DS21143C is the chip manufacturer's datasheet. The synchronization windows are explicitly an example firmware implementation, not a universal receiver guarantee. HCS301-specific secure-learn seed width is high-confidence at 32 bits despite one contradictory 60-bit glossary phrase because three detailed sections agree on 32 bits. Low for any claim about Hiland's exact manufacturer code, derivation, receiver firmware, or whether the requester's unit exposes seed transmission, because none is documented in the reviewed T5502 sources.
source_dates: DS21143C Revision C: June 2011. AN728 current page lists 2015-06-24. HCS301 product and documentation pages retrieved 2026-10-01.
source_claim_type: Protocol and semiconductor behavior: primary manufacturer datasheet. Decoder/reference-design behavior: primary Microchip application note and datasheet examples. Application to T5502 and interpretation of the seed-width inconsistency: clearly identified inference.
relevant_components: HCS301 encoder with EEPROM, controller, KeeLoq block-cipher function, 16-bit synchronization counter, 28-bit serial, configuration/discrimination/overflow state, and four button inputs; external RF transmitter stage driven by PWM; receiver RF front end; decoder firmware; receiver nonvolatile credential table; and OEM provisioning/key-generation process.
hardware_revision_and_markings: DS21143C documents 8-lead PDIP and SOIC packages. Example top marks include HCS301, date code, lot/customer-specific lines, and package identifiers. Revision C lists commercial and industrial temperature ordering variants. A top mark should be recorded in full because abbreviated, remarked, compatible, or counterfeit devices cannot be authenticated from a partial 'HC301' reading. The datasheet revision does not prove a T5502 PCB revision or OEM provisioning.
power_variant: HCS301's specified operating range is 3.5-13.0 V. Its configuration supports low-voltage behavior intended for nominal 6 V versus 9/12 V operation. This makes it compatible with a 12 V transmitter design, but does not prove which battery a particular T5502 uses; a claimed single 3 V cell conflicts with the HCS301 minimum unless other circuitry or a different device is present [uncertain].
rf_profile: HCS301 defines a baseband PWM code word, not the RF carrier. It offers basic pulse elements nominally 400, 200, or 100 microseconds, with selectable alternate-word blanking. Carrier frequency, RF modulation implementation, deviation/bandwidth, and radiated power come from the external transmitter and regional design. Hiland specifies 433.92 MHz for T5502, but this must not be generalized to every HCS301 product.
observable_data: A lawful receive-only observer can characterize preamble/header timing, 66 data-bit framing, nominal baud family, repeated-word behavior, the clear 28-bit serial-bearing fixed portion, button/status changes, low-battery and repeat status behavior, and that the 32-bit hopping portion changes across transmissions. With a deliberately invoked OEM secure-learn mode, the documented seed word can appear in place of the encrypted portion, but ordinary button transmissions do not reveal the counter, discrimination value, overflow state, or key because those fields are encrypted. Observations cannot establish receiver acceptance or key-domain membership.
protected_or_secret_data: The 64-bit per-transmitter crypt key and 64-bit manufacturer code/key-generation domain are secret. The live synchronization state, EEPROM configuration, and secure-learning seed are sensitive even where some are intentionally exposed during an authorized learn transaction. Microchip states that encoder EEPROM is read-protected and not externally accessible; this report omits recovery methods and values.
manufacturer_key_domain_evidence: The public architecture only says a manufacturer code is typically a unique secret 64-bit input used with serial data to generate per-encoder keys; it permits OEM-specific alternatives. Non-secret evidence of domain compatibility must therefore come from OEM part/receiver compatibility documentation, genuine supply-chain provenance, receiver manuals, or written OEM confirmation. Matching serial layout, carrier, enclosure, encoder part number, or seed length is not proof of a common domain.
compatibility_constraints: A receiver must match carrier/modulation and HCS301 timing/framing; recognize the serial; derive or already store the correct per-transmitter key under the same OEM method/domain; validate discrimination and button data; accept the counter under its synchronization policy; map channels correctly; and have capacity/authority to learn the credential. Secure, normal, and simple learning are different strategies, and support for one cannot be inferred from chip identity alone.
variant_conflicts: The key public conflict is DS21143C's isolated '60-bit seed' glossary wording versus the 32-bit EEPROM map, 32-bit seed section, and 32-bit diagram; use 32 bits for HCS301 while flagging the typo. Another frequent ambiguity is confusing the encoder's allowed supply range with a transmitter's battery. Finally, HCS301 compatibility does not imply a universal KeeLoq key domain; resolve at receiver/OEM level.
access_assumption: No enclosure access means only external labels and RF emissions can be examined. Opening the owned transmitter can confirm package and board markings but does not authorize or make secret EEPROM readable. No administrative access means receiver memory and learn policy cannot be inspected. No receiver participation means neither a physical learn button nor an over-the-air learn transaction may occur. No RF reach additionally prevents enrollment and supervised acceptance testing.
receiver_dependency: Normal use requires a receiver that has learned the transmitter and can obtain the right crypt key and synchronization state. Microchip's typical learning flow uses two valid sequential transmissions, validates discrimination, then stores serial, key, and counter. Exact implementation is receiver firmware dependent. A seed is useful only when the receiver deliberately supports the matching secure-learn derivation.
receiver_make_model_firmware: Unknown [uncertain]. It is essential because Microchip expressly allows multiple learning strategies and adjustable synchronization windows. Identify it from authorized records, exterior labels, OEM manuals, or an installer; do not infer firmware behavior from the HCS301 alone.
physical_access_vs_receiver_participatio: A receiver can participate through a documented over-the-air learning sequence without its enclosure being opened. Conversely, merely possessing/opening the transmitter does not enroll another credential. Supported duplication means receiver-authorized provisioning of a new transmitter, not passive transmitter-only copying.
existing_authorized_remote_required: Receiver-dependent: typically yes for remote-triggered self-learning, but not necessarily for an administrator/installer invoking the receiver's local learn function or OEM service.
enrollment_method_and_authority: Use the exact receiver/OEM manual. The authorized administrator, owner, or installer places the decoder into learn mode and enrolls a genuine compatible transmitter through its documented normal or secure process. Microchip describes architectural examples, not end-user authority or a universal button sequence.
credential_semantics: A legitimate result is a new unique transmitter credential accepted and stored by the receiver, a genuine vendor-provisioned compatible credential, or a migrated receiver domain. It is not an independent cryptographic clone created from observed code words. Copying only the public serial would collide in identity but would not supply the valid changing encrypted portion.
receiver_memory_and_revocation: Microchip states maximum learned transmitters depends on decoder EEPROM; no universal HCS301 capacity exists. Exact slot count, overwrite policy, and revocation/reset behavior are receiver-specific [uncertain]. Maintain an inventory, remove lost transmitters using the OEM procedure, and avoid unplanned full-memory erase.
legitimate_routes: Obtain a genuine OEM-domain-compatible replacement and enroll it through the receiver's documented learn mode.
Use an authorized installer or OEM service that can identify the receiver domain and supply/provision the correct unique transmitter.
Use documented remote-triggered learning where the receiver supports it and an enrolled authorized transmitter is present.
Migrate the receiver/radio subsystem and reissue new credentials if legacy provisioning is unavailable or unverifiable.
prerequisites: Ownership/authorization, confirmed transmitter and receiver identities, exact receiver manual/firmware behavior, correct frequency and OEM provisioning domain, an available credential slot, and either an existing authorized remote or administrator/installer access as required by the receiver.
equipment_or_service_needed: Receive-only SDR or spectrum/timing instrument for characterization, macro photography for identity, and an OEM-approved replacement plus authorized receiver/installer service for enrollment. No cryptographic recovery or invasive extraction equipment is part of a legitimate route.
expected_outcomes: Protocol characterization can confirm consistency with HCS301 framing but not the secret domain. Authorized enrollment yields a separate functioning credential. OEM provisioning yields a transmitter compatible with the receiver's domain. Receiver migration restores maintainable access with new credentials.
limitations: The chip datasheet describes a building block and typical decoder, not Hiland's confidential provisioning, the requester's receiver policy, or every firmware variation. Passive signals cannot prove key ownership or derive an accepted independent credential. Seed availability and meaning depend on deliberate OEM configuration. Product age, patents, component availability, and region may constrain service.
cost_or_effort_band: Receive-only characterization: low to medium. Genuine replacement/enrollment: low to medium. Authorized OEM provisioning: medium and availability-dependent. Receiver migration: medium to high. Exact local pricing is unknown [uncertain].
route_classification: Protocol characterization supporting authorized replacement, enrollment, vendor provisioning, interoperability assessment, or receiver migration. RF-only independent cryptographic duplication is unsupported.
product_status_and_authenticity: Microchip's current product page indexes HCS301 as In Production, but a remotely purchased chip or assembled transmitter still requires genuine-source verification. Prefer traceable OEM/authorized stock, verify package marks and lot provenance, and use a return policy tied to receiver compatibility. Generic 'HCS301 clone' advertising does not establish authentic silicon or a matching OEM key domain.
feasibility_without_receiver: Without physical receiver access but with a supported over-the-air learning mode, authorized enrollment may be possible and still entails receiver participation. With no receiver participation at all, observing normal HCS301 transmissions is insufficient to create a new accepted credential because the receiver must recognize the serial, use the correct key/domain, and maintain counter state. An OEM may provision a replacement from its records, but final acceptance still depends on the receiver's existing policy and may require enrollment [uncertain].
confidence: High for HCS301 architecture and the insufficiency of ordinary observed transmissions, based on DS21143C. High that the HCS301 seed is 32 bits despite the isolated 60-bit typo. Moderate for generalized receiver behavior because the synchronization and learning flows are explicitly typical/configurable. Low for T5502-specific configuration until its IC, receiver, and OEM documentation are confirmed.
legal_or_authorization_notes: Access-control credentials may implicate computer-misuse, burglary-tool, privacy, radio, lease, employment, or common-property rules depending on jurisdiction. Restrict work to systems you own or are expressly authorized to administer; seek professional legal advice where authority is contested or testing could affect others.
operational_risks: Repeated presses away from the receiver advance the counter; enough advancement may trigger multi-operation resynchronization or rejection under receiver-specific windows. Learn-mode mistakes may enroll the wrong serial, consume slots, erase memory, or lock out users. Unintended door/gate motion creates safety hazards. Publishing serial captures, seed transactions, or detailed board images can leak security-relevant metadata.
enrollment_side_effects: The receiver will store or update serial, derived/stored crypt key, and synchronization state. Firmware may require two sequential messages, append a slot, overwrite an entry, or clear credentials; only the receiver manual controls. Existing credentials and all channels must be checked after any change.
prohibited_actionable_details_omitted: Yes. Key or seed extraction, cryptographic attack, rolling-code defeat, replay, brute force, invasive readout, and unauthorized-access instructions are omitted.
stop_conditions: Stop if ownership/authority is unclear; the receiver model or manual is unknown; testing would target third-party traffic; a procedure could erase all credentials without recovery; counter advancement begins causing failures; package identity is ambiguous; or an enrollment attempt produces unintended operation. Use the OEM, authorized installer/locksmith, or legal counsel instead.
recommended_next_steps: Confirm the encoder top mark and PCB revision with clear photographs, without probing protected memory.
Use receive-only capture of a minimal number of owned-transmitter presses to check carrier and framing consistency, not to recover credentials.
Identify the receiver make/model/firmware and obtain its exact manual; determine whether it uses normal, secure, or another OEM learning policy.
Ask Hiland or an authorized distributor for written confirmation of the genuine replacement model and receiver-domain compatibility.
Enroll a unique replacement under owner/installer supervision, then inventory, test, and if necessary revoke credentials.
questions_for_owner_or_vendor: Is the IC marking exactly HCS301, including suffix/date/lot lines, and is the device SOIC or PDIP?
Which receiver model and firmware accepts this transmitter, and which learning strategy does it implement?
Is the replacement provisioned for the identical OEM manufacturer-code/key-generation domain?
Does the receiver support remote self-learning, local learning, secure learning, or only installer provisioning?
How many credential slots exist, and does learning append, overwrite, or erase?
What is the documented revocation and recovery procedure if enrollment fails?
rollback_and_acceptance_test: Inventory and verify all current remotes before change; retain the original remote and receiver configuration/installer records. Conduct enrollment with the gate/door safety zone clear and an administrator/manual-release option present. Accept only if the new remote works once on every intended channel, does not actuate unintended channels, every pre-existing authorized remote still works, revoked/lost remotes remain rejected, and normal operation persists after a power cycle where the manual permits that test. If memory or synchronization behavior deviates from documentation, stop and have an authorized installer restore the documented state.
